newsitem.title: IRAQ: Over 750,000 Iraqi children are malnourished - U.N.
newsitem.headline: Over 750,000 Iraqi children are malnourished - U.N.

text.p: The United Nations says over 750,000 Iraqi children do not have enough to eat, a deficiency that could result in the emergence of a stunted generation in Iraq.

According to the latest U.N. nutritional status report on Iraqi children, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters on Tuesday, chronic malnutrition among children under five, shown by low height for age, had reached 27 per cent of Iraq's three million children.
The survey, published on June 1, was conducted jointly during April by the U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF, the World Food Programme and Iraq's health ministry.

It focused on children in the centre and south of Iraq and excluded Kurdish governorates in the north currently outside central government control where the situation according to the report is relatively better.
"Findings from the survey highlight the alarming level of malnutrition in the centre and south," Philippe Heffinck, UNICEF representative in Iraq, told Reuters.

"It shows that there has been a gradual shift of big portions of the young population to malnutrition. Even those who were doing relatively well in the past are slipping gradually to malnutrition," he said.
Chronic malnutrition has long term implications on a child's physical and mental development. Heffinck said it would be difficult to reverse once a child was two or three years of age.
"This will affect the mental and physical growth of children...At schools they will not fare so well; there will be more dropouts," Heffinck said.
"This situation is a direct result from a combination of factors including adverse economic conditions, poor health or insufficient food, and lack of proper care," said the report.

The report said malnutrition was almost non-existent in Iraq prior to U.N. trade sanctions imposed for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait. It afflicted around nine per cent of the child population a year after sanctions, it added.

Most at risk were children under two years old, said the report, and its compilers feared that stunted children would grow to be stunted adults "with the continuation of the same detrimental process on their childhood."

Other forms of malnutrition like wasting and underweight seen in at least 25 per cent of Iraq's child population could easily be reversed if economic and health conditions were improved, the report said.

Heffinck said he hoped Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations would help to address the situation. Iraq said on Friday it had completed the oil exports under the six-month deal and was awaiting a U.N. Security Council offer to renew the pact.
Iraq has repeatedly complained about delays in the arrival of humanitarian supplies under the deal.
